beats.intro: Chapter one, lesson one. What amino acids are, and the one shape they all share. [[plate]]Picture a dinner plate: an egg, a glass of milk, a spoonful of beans. [[zoom]]Every one of them is full of protein. And protein, as we are about to see, is a long chain built from small, repeating pieces. [[units]]Those pieces are the amino acids. Today we meet them, learn their general structure, and draw the map for the whole chapter.
beats.bricks: [[bricks]]An amino acid is a structural unit of protein, a building block. Think of a tower made of bricks. The tower is the protein, and each brick is an amino acid. [[chain]]The protein is a long chain of them. [[acid]]How do we get the bricks back? By hydrolysis, which means breaking bonds with water. Boiling the protein with acid does it. [[alkali]]So does boiling it with alkali. [[enzyme]]And so do enzymes, which is exactly what happens in your gut after a meal. [[free]]Either way, the protein falls apart into free amino acids. Egg, milk and beans all end up as the same small set of pieces.
beats.count: [[twenty]]How many different bricks are there? Twenty known amino acids make up our proteins. [[sel]]Add one more, selenocysteine, and the count becomes twenty-one. [[shelf]]Twenty is the number to remember. Some of these amino acids are tiny, others carry rings, but every one of them is built to the same plan.
beats.plan: [[ca]]Here is that plan. In the middle sits one carbon atom, the alpha carbon. That is why these are called alpha amino acids. [[amino]]On one side, an amino group, written N H two. [[carboxyl]]On the other side, a carboxyl group, written C O O H. [[h]]Below the carbon, a single hydrogen atom. [[r]]And on top, the side chain, called R. [[three]]So three named parts: the amino group, the carboxyl group, and R. [[char]]The first two follow the same pattern in all of them, with one bent exception, proline, which we meet in lesson two. R is the part that is characteristic of each amino acid. It is what makes one amino acid different from another.
beats.rgroup: [[gly]]The simplest case is glycine. Its side chain R is just one hydrogen atom, so there is almost nothing there. [[ala]]Alanine comes next. Its R is a methyl group: one carbon with three hydrogens. [[ser]]Serine has a methyl group with a hydroxyl on the end. [[cover]]Cover the R, and the three are twins: the same carbon, the same amino group, the same carboxyl group. [[swap]]Uncover it, and each is a different amino acid. Swap the R, and you swap the amino acid. [[more]]Bigger groups, rings, sulfur, charges: all of these are possible. The next lesson sorts them.
beats.ion: [[plain]]One small aside, which the slides draw for glycine and alanine. [[charged]]In the watery fluid of the body, the amino group usually picks up a hydrogen ion, and is written N H three plus. The carboxyl group gives one away, and is written C O O minus. [[same]]Same atoms, with the charges that body fluid gives them. You will see both ways of drawing it, so do not let that confuse you.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which part of an amino acid is different from one amino acid to another?
beats.card: [[card]]Let's put it all on one card. One amino acid sits at the centre, with its alpha carbon, amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and R. [[tabs]]Around it are four tabs, because there are four ways to classify amino acids. [[structural]]Structural: by the shape of R. [[chemical]]Chemical: by the amino and carboxyl groups, and so by the electric charge. [[nutritional]]Nutritional: by whether we must eat it. [[metabolic]]And metabolic: by what the body does with its carbon skeleton. [[next]]The next three lessons open this card, one tab at a time.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which classification sorts amino acids by whether the diet must supply them?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Amino acids are the building blocks of protein, and acid, alkali or enzymes release them by hydrolysis. [[s2]]There are twenty of them, twenty-one with selenocysteine. [[s3]]Each has an alpha carbon carrying an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain R. R is what differs, and glycine, with just a hydrogen, is the simplest. [[s4]]And there are four ways to classify them: structural, chemical, nutritional and metabolic. [[end]]Now try the practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That's the end of chapter one, lesson one.
